candidates.name: C11 draft: pointer/integer conversions and intptr_t/uintptr_t
candidates.reason: Its pointer-preserving integer types provide a concrete conversion contract for exposing addresses to Swift integer arithmetic and matching C pointer-sized integer parameters.
candidates.application_scope: Address representation, explicit conversions, and C interoperability.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: The types are optional; their round-trip guarantee covers valid void pointers, while arbitrary address edits and resulting pointer validity remain implementation-dependent.
candidates.date_evidence: N1570 is dated April 12, 2011; sections 6.3.2.3 and 7.20.1.4 were read.

candidates.name: Bit Twiddling Hacks: masked bit merging
candidates.reason: Its masked integer-bit merge supplies a small mechanism for inserting or replacing pointer tags once Swift exposes a suitable integer address representation.
candidates.application_scope: Integer operations underlying pointer tagging; alignment-mask operations are adjacent supporting material.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Applying it to addresses is a translation inference: tag bits must be available on the target ABI, and conversion back to a usable pointer needs a separate contract.
candidates.date_evidence: The original source dates the mask-merging entry to February 9, 2006; no claim is made that the entire current page predates the cutoff.

raw_response:
Two candidates are directly useful for this design problem.

1. C11 draft: pointer/integer conversions and intptr_t/uintptr_t
https://port70.net/~nsz/c/c11/n1570.html
The C11 model is a reference for giving Swift an explicit address-to-integer conversion that supports arithmetic and C integer parameters. The optional types preserve valid void-pointer round trips; edited addresses still need platform-specific validity rules. Evidence: N1570, April 12, 2011, sections 6.3.2.3 and 7.20.1.4.

2. Bit Twiddling Hacks: masked bit merging
https://graphics.stanford.edu/~seander/bithacks.html
The masked merge can be translated into pointer-tag insertion or replacement after an address is available as an integer. This is my application inference, not a demonstrated Swift implementation. Only ABI-available bits may hold tags, and pointer reconstruction remains a separate concern. The entry is explicitly attributed to February 9, 2006.

Both were discovered in the opened catalogue https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c and then checked in its outgoing sources. I inspected unsafe-swift from a Swift catalogue but did not retain it: its examples did not establish the required address-integer operation. These are transfer candidates, with no deployment or usefulness claim.
limitations: This is catalogue discovery plus translation by an internal model, not a human study.
Only the assigned rules and C23 prefix were read from the local research materials; no gold, A run, other prefix, target proposal, or repository history was read.
Model pretraining knowledge cannot be erased; memory leakage is not controlled.
All discovery queries targeted awesome lists or named catalogue repositories. Search engines returned some non-catalogue results, which were not used for discovery or opened.

Two web open attempts returned DisabledError; ordinary unauthenticated Python HTTP fetches subsequently obtained the catalogue links and unsafe-swift README. No login, paid API, installed tool, or access-control bypass was used.
opened_pages counts all 13 explicit open/fetch attempts, including repeat URLs and two failed attempts; finds within already-opened pages are recorded in sections_read and do not add new pages.
Live catalogue availability before the cutoff is unknown. Candidate date claims are limited to the dated standard and explicitly dated bit-merging mechanism.

The sources do not establish the exact Swift API surface or guarantee that arbitrary pointer tagging is valid. No finished Swift address-manipulation component was established under this discovery route.
